Features, hierarchy and the whole model

Source: vignettes/features-hierarchy.Rmd
features-hierarchy.Rmd

Measuring each feature

Every measure of every feature

Function: vp_feature_table()

The question. Which features does everything else depend on? Which ones depend on many others? Which ones decide the most?

vp_feature_table() gives one row per feature that can vary, with one column per measure. Each measure is given in words, with an example, and as a formula, in the notation of this box:

Notation of the formulas. VV is the set of features that can vary (the nodes of the graphs) and n=|V|n = |V| their number; |X||X| is the number of elements of a set XX. For two features ff and gg of VV:

  • f⇒gf \Rightarrow g: ff requires gg (an arrow of the requires graph);

  • f#gf \mathbin{\#} g: ff excludes gg (a line of the excludes graph);

  • f∨gf \vee g: every product has ff or gg (a line of the at-least-one graph);

  • f→gf \to g: an arrow of the skeleton SS, the requires graph without the arrows that follow from others (The skeleton), and dS(f,g)d_S(f, g) the number of arrows of the shortest chain of SS from ff to gg (∞\infty when there is none).

The table has fifteen columns, so here they are a few at a time, picked with select(). Each group comes with a table that gives its formula and a one-line meaning, followed by a detailed explanation of every column on the drawings of the band.

Four counts 

ft <- vp_feature_table(band)
ft |> select(feature, required_by, requires, excludes, atleastone)
#> # A tibble: 11 x 5
#>    feature            required_by requires excludes atleastone
#>    <chr>                    <int>    <int>    <int>      <int>
#>  1 Screen                       6        2        1          1
#>  2 TouchScreen                  0        3        1          0
#>  3 OLED                         6        2        1          1
#>  4 CapacityButton               6        2        1          1
#>  5 ContactlessPayment           0        1        0          0
#>  6 MovementFilter               0        4        3          0
#>  7 HeartRateSensor              1        0        1          0
#>  8 BLEv40                       1        3        2          0
#>  9 BLEv42                       0        4        3          0
#> 10 BT40                         0        0        7          3
#> 11 NFC                          1        0        0          0
Column Formula Meaning
required_by |{g∈V:g⇒f}||\{g \in V : g \Rightarrow f\}| How many features require this one (its sensitivity).
requires |{g∈V:f⇒g}||\{g \in V : f \Rightarrow g\}| How many features it requires.
excludes |{g∈V:f#g}||\{g \in V : f \mathbin{\#} g\}| How many features it excludes (its conflict degree).
atleastone |{g∈V:f∨g}||\{g \in V : f \vee g\}| How many features it is joined to in the at-least-one graph.

The figure is the requires graph of the band, and the figure its excludes graph; the links of MovementFilter are thick. Every count of this group can be read on them.

The requires graph of the Mi Band 3. The four thick arrows leave MovementFilter: selecting it selects BLEv40 and the three features of the atomic set of the screen (dashed box).
The excludes graph of the Mi Band 3. The three thick lines join MovementFilter to the features it excludes: HeartRateSensor, BLEv42 and BT40.

required_by: how many features depend on this one. Count the arrows that arrive at the feature in the figure. Six arrive at Screen: from TouchScreen, MovementFilter, BLEv40, BLEv42, and from OLED and CapacityButton, the other two members of its atomic set. Those six features form the impact set of the screen: if the screen is removed, renamed or given a new requirement, all six are affected Abate et al. (2009). The measure is also called the sensitivity of a feature. Because the requires graph is complete, the count includes the features that depend on it through a chain: MovementFilter reaches the screen only through BLEv40, and it is counted. Use it to find the features that deserve the most careful review and the most testing: a mistake in them spreads to many others.

requires: how many features this one depends on. Count the arrows that leave the feature. Four leave MovementFilter: BLEv40, Screen, OLED and CapacityButton. So selecting the movement filter brings four features along, and four features can break it: if any of them changes, the movement filter may stop working. Use it to find fragile features, and the features that a user cannot select without accepting many others.

excludes: how many features this one rules out. Count the lines of the feature in the figure: three for MovementFilter, seven for BT40. It is the conflict degree of the feature: what selecting it costs in lost choices. A feature that excludes almost everything is available only in a small corner of the products, which is worth checking against the intention of whoever wrote it.

atleastone: how many features leaving this one out forces in. Count the lines of the feature in the at-least-one graph (the figure): BT40 has three, to the three features of the atomic set of the screen, because every band has a screen or classic Bluetooth. It is NA when the run had no or_graph = TRUE. Why it matters: these are the features a user cannot simply refuse. In a configurator, leaving out one of them forces another in, so a high count marks a feature whose “no” has consequences that users do not expect; for testing, each line removes one combination (“neither”) that no product can have.

The at-least-one graph of the Mi Band 3. A dotted green line joins two features of which every band has at least one.

What a decision settles 

ft |> select(feature, decision_power, decision_power_off, isolated)
#> # A tibble: 11 x 4
#>    feature            decision_power decision_power_off isolated
#>    <chr>                       <dbl>              <dbl> <lgl>   
#>  1 Screen                        0.3                0.7 FALSE   
#>  2 TouchScreen                   0.4                0   FALSE   
#>  3 OLED                          0.3                0.7 FALSE   
#>  4 CapacityButton                0.3                0.7 FALSE   
#>  5 ContactlessPayment            0.1                0   FALSE   
#>  6 MovementFilter                0.7                0   FALSE   
#>  7 HeartRateSensor               0.1                0.1 FALSE   
#>  8 BLEv40                        0.5                0.1 FALSE   
#>  9 BLEv42                        0.7                0   FALSE   
#> 10 BT40                          0.7                0.3 FALSE   
#> 11 NFC                           0                  0.1 FALSE
Column Formula Meaning
decision_power requires(f)+excludes(f)n−1\dfrac{\text{requires}(f) + \text{excludes}(f)}{n - 1} The share of the other features that selecting it decides.
decision_power_off required_by(f)+atleastone(f)n−1\dfrac{\text{required\_by}(f) + \text{atleastone}(f)}{n - 1} The share of the other features that leaving it out decides.
isolated required_by+requires+excludes+atleastone=0\text{required\_by} + \text{requires} + \text{excludes} + \text{atleastone} = 0 TRUE for a feature in no graph.

decision_power: what selecting the feature settles. Selecting the movement filter settles 4 features by the arrows of the figure (they are selected too) and 3 by the lines of the figure (they cannot be selected). Of the other 10 features of the band, 7 are decided: the decision power is (4+3)/10=0.7(4 + 3)/10 = 0.7. Selecting NFC settles nothing: it has no arrow leaving it and no line, so its decision power is 0. The measure says how much a yes settles; averaged over all features (mean_decision_power, The whole model in numbers) it says how fast a configuration session collapses. It is not, by itself, the best order in which to ask the questions, because the answer can be no (see the box “Decision power is not the order in which to ask” below). Mann and Rock define the same ratio on the written model Mann and Rock (2011).

decision_power_off: what leaving the feature out settles. Leaving a feature out works the other way round. Every feature whose arrow arrives at it must be left out too (it could not have it), and every feature joined to it by an at-least-one line must be selected. Leaving out Screen rules out the 6 features whose arrows arrive at it in the figure and forces BT40 in, by the line of the figure: (6+1)/10=0.7(6 + 1)/10 = 0.7. Leaving out NFC rules out ContactlessPayment, which requires it: 1/10=0.11/10 = 0.1. It is NA without or_graph = TRUE. Why it matters: in a configuration session “no” is as frequent as “yes”, often more. A feature whose refusal settles much (the screen, here) is a feature whose removal from a product, or from the product line, reaches many others: a high value marks the features that cannot be dropped lightly.

isolated: is the feature in no graph? TRUE when the feature has no arrow and no line at all. No feature of the band is isolated; BusyBox has 38. As far as relationships between two features go, such a feature is free. Some are truly independent; others are constrained only by rules over three or more features, which the graphs do not show; a few may be left-overs that nothing uses any more. Why it matters: isolated features are the cheapest to test (they can be combined freely), the first suspects in a clean-up of dead options, and, when many, a hint that the model holds constraints the graphs cannot see.

Measures on the skeleton

The last columns look at the skeleton only (the figure): the arrows that do not follow from others, close to what was written. On the skeleton, each arrow is one step, so it makes sense to talk about how far apart two features are, which in the complete graph, where every requirement is a direct arrow, would always be one step.

The skeleton of the Mi Band 3 (the atomic set of the screen is one node). The thick arrows are the only chain of two steps; BLEv40, highlighted, is the only feature between two others.
ft |> select(feature, level, direct_required_by, direct_requires)
#> # A tibble: 11 x 4
#>    feature            level direct_required_by direct_requires
#>    <chr>              <int>              <int>           <int>
#>  1 Screen                 0                  3               0
#>  2 TouchScreen            1                  0               1
#>  3 OLED                   0                  3               0
#>  4 CapacityButton         0                  3               0
#>  5 ContactlessPayment     1                  0               1
#>  6 MovementFilter         2                  0               1
#>  7 HeartRateSensor        0                  1               0
#>  8 BLEv40                 1                  1               1
#>  9 BLEv42                 1                  0               2
#> 10 BT40                   0                  0               0
#> 11 NFC                    0                  1               0
ft |> select(feature, betweenness, closeness_out, closeness_in, harmonic)

Column Formula Meaning
level 00 if ff has no arrow in SS; else 1+max⁡f→glevel(g)1 + \max_{f \to g} \text{level}(g) Its layer in the hierarchy.
direct_required_by |{g:g→f}||\{g : g \to f\}| The features that require it directly.
direct_requires |{g:f→g}||\{g : f \to g\}| The features it requires directly.
betweenness ∑s≠f≠tσst(f)σst\displaystyle\sum_{s \neq f \neq t} \frac{\sigma_{st}(f)}{\sigma_{st}}, where σst\sigma_{st} counts the shortest chains of SS from ss to tt and σst(f)\sigma_{st}(f) those that pass through ff How many chains of requirements pass through it.
closeness_out k∑gdS(f,g)\dfrac{k}{\sum_{g} d_S(f, g)}, over the kk features gg that ff reaches One over the average number of steps to what it requires.
closeness_in k∑gdS(g,f)\dfrac{k}{\sum_{g} d_S(g, f)}, over the kk features gg that reach ff One over the average number of steps from what requires it.
harmonic ∑g≠f1dS(f,g)\displaystyle\sum_{g \neq f} \frac{1}{d_S(f, g)}, with 1/∞=01/\infty = 0 The sum of one over the steps to each requirement.
atomic_set The first feature of its atomic set, if it is in one.

In all of them an atomic set counts as one node, as in the figure, and its members share its values.

level: the layer of the feature. A feature that needs nothing is at level 0 (the screen, the heart-rate sensor, BT40, NFC); a feature whose direct requirements are all at level 0 is at level 1 (TouchScreen, ContactlessPayment, BLEv40, BLEv42); MovementFilter, which needs BLEv40, is at level 2. The level is the length of the longest chain of requirements that starts at the feature, so it is the number of steps of the longest explanation of why selecting it forces something. Why it matters: features of level 0 are the foundations, to be built and stabilised first; a high level marks a feature that rests on a tall stack of others, so it is more likely to be broken by changes below it and harder to explain to users. A configurator asks about features in the order of their levels (A safe order for the questions). Levels, depth and the longest chain draws the levels and uses them.

direct_required_by and direct_requires: the arrows of the skeleton. Count the arrows that arrive at, or leave, the feature in the figure. Three arrive at the screen, from TouchScreen, BLEv40 and BLEv42, against six in the complete graph: the other three are MovementFilter, which reaches the screen only through BLEv40, and OLED and CapacityButton, which are the screen itself as far as choices go. BLEv42 has two direct requirements, the screen and the heart-rate sensor. The difference between a count and its direct version is what the chains add: a feature with many dependants but few direct ones is a hub by inheritance, which vp_genuine_hubs() (below) examines.

betweenness: is the feature a gateway? Some features are not the beginning of a requirement, nor its end, but a step in the middle: a feature ff requires a feature gg only through them. Betweenness counts how often a feature is such a step. It is measured on the skeleton, where each arrow is one step, in three steps:

  1. Take every pair of features ss and tt such that ss requires tt through a chain of two arrows or more of the skeleton. (A direct arrow has nothing in between, so it gives no point to anybody.)

  2. Find the shortest chain from ss to tt.

  3. Give one point to every feature in the middle of that chain. If several chains are equally short, share the point among them: with two such chains, each feature in the middle of one of them gets half a point.

The betweenness of a feature is the sum of its points: in the formula of the table, σst\sigma_{st} is the number of shortest chains from ss to tt, and σst(f)\sigma_{st}(f) the number of those that pass through ff.

On the band. The pairs of step 1 are the arrows of the requires graph that are not in the skeleton, between different nodes: those that need a chain. vp_implied_requires() (The skeleton) lists them, and vp_explain_requires() gives the chain:

vp_implied_requires(band)
#> # A tibble: 1 x 3
#>   from           to     via   
#>   <chr>          <chr>  <chr> 
#> 1 MovementFilter Screen BLEv40
vp_explain_requires(band, "MovementFilter", "Screen") |> filter(route == 1)
#> # A tibble: 2 x 5
#>   route  step from           link     to    
#>   <int> <int> <chr>          <chr>    <chr> 
#> 1     1     1 MovementFilter requires BLEv40
#> 2     1     2 BLEv40         requires Screen

There is a single pair, and a single chain: MovementFilter → BLEv40 → the screen (the thick arrows of the figure). BLEv40 is in its middle, so it gets the only point: its betweenness is 1, and every other feature has 0. The screen is the most required feature of the band, yet its betweenness is 0: it ends chains, it does not relay them. A feature with a high betweenness is a gateway: the point through which indirect requirements pass, and where implicit dependencies come from.

On a bigger band. The Mi Band 8, the last generation of the history of Reading the results, has longer chains:

vp_feature_table(history$model[[7]]) |>
  filter(betweenness > 0, is.na(atomic_set) | atomic_set == feature) |>
  select(feature, betweenness, required_by) |>
  arrange(desc(betweenness))
#> # A tibble: 7 x 3
#>   feature            betweenness required_by
#>   <chr>                    <dbl>       <int>
#> 1 TouchScreen                 16          14
#> 2 AMOLED                      15          11
#> 3 Photoplethysmogram           9           4
#> 4 SpO2                         5           1
#> 5 OLED                         3           4
#> 6 ContactlessPayment           3           3
#> 7 BLEv40                       2           1

Being required and being a gateway are different things. Compare two features of the table above:

vp_feature_table(history$model[[7]]) |>
  filter(feature %in% c("AMOLED", "HeartRateSensor")) |>
  select(feature, required_by, betweenness)
#> # A tibble: 2 x 3
#>   feature         required_by betweenness
#>   <chr>                 <int>       <dbl>
#> 1 AMOLED                   11          15
#> 2 HeartRateSensor          16           0

The heart-rate sensor is required by more features than the AMOLED screen (16 against 11), and yet its betweenness is 0 while the AMOLED screen’s is 15. The figure shows why.

The skeleton of the Mi Band 8, with the betweenness of each node in brackets. The AMOLED screen (yellow) relays the chains from the six features below it to the three above it, except those from Infrared, whose shortest way to the touch screen goes through ContactlessPayment (thick arrows).

The heart-rate sensor is at the top. It needs nothing, so every chain that reaches it ends there. It is never in the middle of a chain, and gets no point.

The AMOLED screen is in the middle (an atomic set of five features, one node of the figure). Six features reach it by chains of arrows: Photoplethysmogram, SpO2, Infrared, BLEv50, BLEv51 and BLEv52. Beyond it lie three: the touch screen, the screen and the heart-rate sensor. That makes 6×3=186 \times 3 = 18 pairs whose chains could pass through the AMOLED screen. For three of them, those that start at Infrared, the shortest chain does not: Infrared reaches the touch screen in two steps through ContactlessPayment (thick arrows), and in three through the AMOLED screen. Only the shortest chain counts, so the AMOLED screen gets 18−3=1518 - 3 = 15 points. (The touch screen, just above it, gets 16: almost every chain of the band goes through it on its way to the screen or to the heart-rate sensor.)

In short: required_by says how many features depend on a feature; betweenness says how many dependencies travel through it.

Why it matters. Changing the heart-rate sensor affects its 16 dependants. Changing the requirements of the AMOLED screen (say, it no longer needs the touch screen) breaks 15 indirect requirements at once, of features that never mention the touch screen themselves: it rewires everything below it. So a gateway is riskier to edit than its required_by suggests. Menus and switches of whole subsystems typically show up as gateways. Betweenness is computed on the skeleton because in the complete requires graph every requirement is a direct arrow, every chain has one step, and every betweenness would be 0.

closeness_out: how far away the requirements are. Some features list everything they need in their own declaration; others need features that are only reached through a chain. closeness_out tells them apart, in four steps:

  1. In the skeleton, follow the arrows from the feature and list every node that can be reached: these are its requirements (an atomic set is one node, so it is counted once). Call their number kk.

  2. For each node reached, count the arrows of the shortest way to it: its distance, dSd_S.

  3. Average the distances: add them up and divide by kk.

  4. Closeness is 1 divided by that average distance.

Why divide 1 by the average? So that the number grows when the requirements are closer. An average distance of 1 (every requirement is a direct arrow) gives closeness 1/1=11/1 = 1, the highest possible value; an average of 2 gives 1/2=0.51/2 = 0.5; an average of 4 gives 1/4=0.251/4 = 0.25. The farther the requirements, the smaller the closeness. (Since the average is the sum of the distances divided by kk, dividing 1 by it is the same as dividing kk by the sum of the distances, which is how the formula in the table above is written: k/∑dSk / \sum d_S.)

For MovementFilter, in the figure:

Step Value
1. Nodes reached BLEv40; the screen (with OLED and CapacityButton, its atomic set) k=2k = 2
2. Distances BLEv40: 1 arrow; the screen: 2 arrows, through BLEv40 1 and 2
3. Average distance (sum of the distances) / kk=(1+2)/2= (1 + 2) / 2 1.51.5
4. closeness_out 1/1 / (average distance) =1/1.5= 1 / 1.5 0.667\mathbf{0.667}

The same last step, written as in the formula: k/(sum of the distances)=2/3=0.667k / (\text{sum of the distances}) = 2 / 3 = 0.667.

BLEv42 reaches its two requirements, the screen and the heart-rate sensor, in one step each: k=2k = 2, sum 2, closeness 2/2=12/2 = 1. So does TouchScreen, with one requirement at one step: 1/1=11/1 = 1. A low value marks a feature whose requirements are mostly indirect: reading its own declaration tells little about what it drags in, so it is a likely source of surprises for users. It is NA for a feature that requires nothing (k=0k = 0), and it does not say how many requirements there are: one requirement at one step, and ten at one step each, both give 1 (harmonic, below, does).

closeness_in: how far away the dependants are. The same, in the other direction: the features that reach this one. The screen is reached by TouchScreen, BLEv40 and BLEv42 in one step and by MovementFilter in two: 4/(1+1+1+2)=0.84/(1 + 1 + 1 + 2) = 0.8. A low value marks a hub whose dependants are far away: the case in which those who change the hub are least likely to know who depends on it.

harmonic: how much a feature drags in, the near counting more. closeness_out answers “how far away, on average, are the requirements?”; it does not care how many there are. The harmonic centrality answers a different question: paste0( “how much does selecting the feature drag in, if a direct requirement”, “counts fully and a far one counts less?” ). Its first two steps are those of closeness_out:

  1. In the skeleton, list every node that the feature reaches (its requirements; an atomic set counts once).

  2. For each, count the arrows of the shortest way to it: its distance.

  3. Turn each distance into a weight, 1 divided by the distance: a direct requirement weighs 1/1=11/1 = 1, one at two steps 1/2=0.51/2 = 0.5, one at three steps 1/31/3, and so on. A node that is not reached weighs 0.

  4. Add the weights.

For MovementFilter: BLEv40 at one step weighs 1, the screen at two steps weighs 0.5; harmonic =1+0.5=1.5= 1 + 0.5 = 1.5. Three features of the band show how the two measures differ:

Feature Requirements Distances closeness_out harmonic
TouchScreen the screen 1 1/1=11/1 = 1 1/1=11/1 = 1
BLEv42 the screen, the heart-rate sensor 1 and 1 1/1=11/1 = 1 1/1+1/1=21/1 + 1/1 = 2
MovementFilter BLEv40, the screen 1 and 2 1/1.5=0.6671/1.5 = 0.667 1/1+1/2=1.51/1 + 1/2 = 1.5
Screen nothing NA 0

closeness_out cannot tell TouchScreen from BLEv42: both have their requirements one step away. harmonic can: BLEv42 drags in twice as much. And it ranks MovementFilter in between: it drags in two requirements, but one of them from far.

Which one to use.

closeness_out harmonic
Question How indirect are the requirements? How much does the feature drag in, the near counting more?
Use it to find features whose requirements are hidden behind chains, whatever their number: those whose own declaration tells least about what they bring, the likely sources of surprises. rank features by how much they pull in; compare features that have different numbers of requirements; average or sum over many features.
Advantages A pure measure of distance, easy to read: 1 means “everything is direct”, 0.5 “two steps on average”. Defined for every feature (0 when it requires nothing), so no row is lost in a ranking or an average. Grows with every requirement, and still gives weight to the far ones. The usual choice of network science for graphs in several pieces, like these.
Disadvantages NA for features that require nothing. Blind to how many requirements there are. With one or two requirements it jumps between few values. Mixes number and distance, so one value can mean different things: two requirements at one step and four at two steps both give 2. Grows with the size of the model, so compare features of the same model (divide by n−1n - 1 to compare models).

atomic_set: is the feature one of a group? The first feature of its atomic set (Atomic sets), or NA. The three features of the band’s set are always selected together, so for every measure of the skeleton they are one feature. Why it matters: members of an atomic set are one decision, so a configurator should ask about them once and a test plan should vary them together.

Using it. The table is a tibble, so the usual verbs work. The features that decide most, first:

ft |>
  arrange(desc(decision_power)) |>
  select(feature, decision_power, requires, excludes) |>
  head(4)
#> # A tibble: 4 x 4
#>   feature        decision_power requires excludes
#>   <chr>                   <dbl>    <int>    <int>
#> 1 MovementFilter            0.7        4        3
#> 2 BLEv42                    0.7        4        3
#> 3 BT40                      0.7        0        7
#> 4 BLEv40                    0.5        3        2

Decision power is not the order in which to ask. It is tempting to conclude that a configurator should ask first about the features with the highest decision power. But a question has two answers. The movement filter is in only a quarter of the bands: asked about it, users answer no three times out of four, and a no settles nothing (its decision_power_off is 0).

Heradio et al. compared orders of configuration questions on real models (a Renault car and an e-commerce platform) and found that the fewest questions are needed when the next question is the one whose answer is the most uncertain: the one with the highest entropy, H=−plog⁡2p−(1−p)log⁡2(1−p)H = -p \log_2 p - (1 - p) \log_2 (1 - p), where pp is the share of the valid products that have the feature Heradio et al. (2014). Asking first about the features involved in the most constraints, the closest to decision power, needed more questions. A feature with p=1/2p = 1/2 is the best question: whatever the answer, it halves the products left.

Entropy needs pp, and pp comes from counting the products (with a BDD or a #SAT solver), which the graphs cannot do. For the band, whose 24 products were enumerated for the vignettes, it can be computed:

# the 24 valid bands, one per row
products <- read.csv("data/miband3_products.csv")
ft |>
  mutate(
    p = colMeans(products[feature]),
    entropy = -p * log2(p) - (1 - p) * log2(1 - p)
  ) |>
  select(feature, decision_power, decision_power_off, p, entropy) |>
  arrange(desc(entropy))
#> # A tibble: 11 x 5
#>    feature            decision_power decision_power_off     p entropy
#>    <chr>                       <dbl>              <dbl> <dbl>   <dbl>
#>  1 BLEv40                        0.5                0.1 0.5     1    
#>  2 TouchScreen                   0.4                0   0.375   0.954
#>  3 HeartRateSensor               0.1                0.1 0.625   0.954
#>  4 ContactlessPayment            0.1                0   0.333   0.918
#>  5 NFC                           0                  0.1 0.667   0.918
#>  6 Screen                        0.3                0.7 0.75    0.811
#>  7 OLED                          0.3                0.7 0.75    0.811
#>  8 CapacityButton                0.3                0.7 0.75    0.811
#>  9 MovementFilter                0.7                0   0.25    0.811
#> 10 BLEv42                        0.7                0   0.25    0.811
#> 11 BT40                          0.7                0.3 0.25    0.811

BLEv40, in half of the bands, is the best first question (entropy 1). The three features with the highest decision power, MovementFilter, BLEv42 and BT40, come last: each is in a quarter of the bands. Decision power describes the model; to order the questions of a configurator, use the entropy, recomputed after each answer as the article explains.

On a bigger model the table is where most studies start. For the last month of the BusyBox history, a chart of how many features require each feature against how many it requires shows at a glance the hubs (far right), the demanding features (high up), and the few that are both:

bb <- busybox$model[[nrow(busybox)]]
p <- vp_feature_table(bb) |>
  ggplot(aes(required_by, requires)) +
  geom_jitter(width = 0.15, height = 0.15, alpha = 0.4, colour = "#0B3D91") +
  labs(x = "required by (features)", y = "requires (features)")
BusyBox, 2010-05: one dot per feature. Most features need little and are needed by few (bottom left).

Limits: what this cannot tell you

  • Every count is a count of relationships between two features. A feature that is constrained only by a rule over three or more features (“A needs B or C”) gets nothing from that rule: BLEv42 requires HeartRateSensor in the graphs only because a rule over three features happens to imply it.

  • decision_power is what selecting one feature decides by itself. Two selections together can decide more than the sum of what each decides, through a rule over three features (Configuring).

  • level, direct_required_by, direct_requires, betweenness, closeness_out, closeness_in and harmonic are computed on the skeleton, not on the complete graph: in the complete graph every requirement is one step away, and distances would be meaningless. The skeleton has the limits of The skeleton.

  • For those measures an atomic set counts as one feature: its members get the values of the set.

What a feature requires, excludes, or is required by

Function: vp_required_by()

The question. Which features exactly are behind those numbers?

Four functions list them, each as a tibble with one column, feature:

vp_required_by(band, f) the features that require f: its impact set
vp_requirements(band, f) the features that f requires
vp_conflicts_of(band, f) the features that f excludes
vp_atleastone_of(band, f) the features that leaving f out forces in 
vp_required_by(band, "Screen")
#> # A tibble: 6 x 1
#>   feature       
#>   <chr>         
#> 1 TouchScreen   
#> 2 OLED          
#> 3 CapacityButton
#> 4 MovementFilter
#> 5 BLEv40        
#> 6 BLEv42
vp_conflicts_of(band, "BT40")
#> # A tibble: 7 x 1
#>   feature       
#>   <chr>         
#> 1 Screen        
#> 2 TouchScreen   
#> 3 OLED          
#> 4 CapacityButton
#> 5 MovementFilter
#> 6 BLEv40        
#> 7 BLEv42

Misspell a name, or give a feature that is not a dot of the graphs, and the function says so:

try(vp_required_by(band, "Pedometer"))
#> Error : "Pedometer" is core, so it is not a node of the graphs

Pedometer is core: every band has it, so every feature “requires” it, which says nothing about the choices, and variplex leaves it out of the graphs. (try() only lets the example go on after the error; you do not need it.)

Why it matters. These lists are the everyday questions of whoever maintains a product line: before changing or removing a feature, who depends on it (its impact set); before selecting it, what it brings along and what it rules out. They are the concrete names behind the counts of the feature table, and exact, so a change can be planned on them.

Limits: what this cannot tell you

The lists are complete for relationships between two features: if a feature is not in vp_required_by(band, "Screen"), some valid band has it without a screen. They are silent about rules over three or more features.

Genuine hubs

Function: vp_genuine_hubs()

The question. Is a feature required by many others in its own right, or only because one popular feature requires it?

Suppose a feature qq has a thousand dependants, but almost all of them require qq only because they require some feature pp, and pp requires qq. Then the thousand dependants are really pp’s dependants: qq inherits them. Reviewing qq as if it were central would miss the point; pp is the feature to watch. Abate et al. call this strong dominance Abate et al. (2009): ppdominates qq when pp requires qq and nearly all the other features that require qq also require pp. A hub that no feature dominates is genuine: its dependants reach it by many different ways. vp_genuine_hubs() works in three steps:

  1. Take the most required features (top, 10 by default).

  2. For each of them, qq, and for each feature pp that requires qq, compute the share of the other dependants of qq that also require pp: the column share_through.

  3. If some pp reaches the threshold share (0.9 by default: “nearly all”), qq is dominated by the one with the highest share; otherwise qq is genuine.

On the band the answer is simple:

vp_genuine_hubs(band)
#> # A tibble: 4 x 5
#>   feature         required_by dominated_by       share_through genuine
#>   <chr>                 <int> <chr>                      <dbl> <lgl>  
#> 1 Screen                    4 <NA>                          NA TRUE   
#> 2 HeartRateSensor           1 BLEv42                         1 FALSE  
#> 3 BLEv40                    1 MovementFilter                 1 FALSE  
#> 4 NFC                       1 ContactlessPayment             1 FALSE

The screen is genuine: of the 4 features that require it (the atomic set counts as one), none gathers the others. The heart-rate sensor, BLEv40 and NFC are required by a single feature each, which dominates them trivially: BLEv40 is required only because the movement filter is (the figure). Domination becomes interesting when a hub has many dependants.

The band: the screen (blue) is a genuine hub, reached directly by three features. BLEv40 (yellow) is required only by MovementFilter (thick arrow): its dependants are the movement filter’s, so the movement filter dominates it.

On Linux 3.13, the twelve most required options:

vp_genuine_hubs(linux, top = 12)
#> # A tibble: 12 x 5
#>    feature           required_by dominated_by   share_through genuine
#>    <chr>                   <int> <chr>                  <dbl> <lgl>  
#>  1 NLATTR                   1671 NET                    0.999 FALSE  
#>  2 GENERIC_NET_UTILS        1671 NET                    0.999 FALSE  
#>  3 NET                      1669 <NA>                  NA     TRUE   
#>  4 DEVPORT                  1558 <NA>                  NA     TRUE   
#>  5 PCI                      1351 <NA>                  NA     TRUE   
#>  6 RT_MUTEXES               1002 I2C                    0.996 FALSE  
#>  7 I2C                       997 <NA>                  NA     TRUE   
#>  8 NLS                       909 <NA>                  NA     TRUE   
#>  9 CRYPTO                    895 CRYPTO_ALGAPI2         0.972 FALSE  
#> 10 CRYPTO_ALGAPI2            869 CRYPTO_ALGAPI          0.990 FALSE  
#> 11 CRYPTO_ALGAPI             859 <NA>                  NA     TRUE   
#> 12 NETDEVICES                768 <NA>                  NA     TRUE

NLATTR, the library of netlink attributes, is the most required option of the kernel: 1,767 options require it (the table counts each atomic set once, hence a smaller number). But NET requires it, and of all those options only 2 reach it without requiring NET as well (the figure): share_through is 0.999. NLATTR is required because networking is; NET is the genuine hub. The crypto options show a chain: CRYPTO is dominated by CRYPTO_ALGAPI2, which is dominated by CRYPTO_ALGAPI, which is genuine. Follow dominated_by until a genuine hub to find the feature whose dependants they all are.

Why it matters. The list of the most required features is long and repetitive: many of its entries are there only because they sit below a big hub. The genuine hubs are the short list of features that really hold the model together, the ones whose review pays off. A fixed threshold such as “required by more than 10 % of the features” Sanchez et al. (2026) cannot make that distinction; domination can.

Limits: what this cannot tell you

Dominance is read from the requires graph, so it inherits its limits. The threshold share is a choice: with 0.9, a hub required by 11 features is dominated when 9 of the other 10 also require the same feature. Try other values before drawing conclusions. A feature required by a single feature is always dominated by it, which says little. Only the top most required features are examined.

The warning zone

Function: vp_warning_zone()

The question. Which features are both highly required and highly demanding?

Such features are costly in both directions: many things break when they change, and many things can break them Sanchez et al. (2026). vp_warning_zone() returns the rows of the feature table in the top tenth (top = 0.1) for both required_by and requires. The band is too small to have any. Linux 3.13 has 140 options in the zone; the most extreme ones first:

wz <- vp_warning_zone(linux)
nrow(wz)
#> [1] 140
wz |>
  arrange(desc(required_by * requires)) |>
  select(feature, required_by, requires) |>
  head(5)
#> # A tibble: 5 x 3
#>   feature         required_by requires
#>   <chr>                 <int>    <int>
#> 1 SND_SOC_DA7210           63      115
#> 2 SND_SOC_WM5100           63      115
#> 3 SND_SOC_MAX9850          63      115
#> 4 SND_SOC_WM8900           63      115
#> 5 SND_SOC_WM8991           63      115
Linux 3.13: one dot per option, on logarithmic axes (plus one, so that 0 can be drawn). The dashed lines are the thresholds of the top tenth: required by at least 11 options, and requiring at least 26. The options of the warning zone (red) are beyond both lines: the upper-right corner. The hubs far to the right need little; the options at the top left are needed by nobody.

The cluster at the top of the zone is a family of sound codec drivers (SND_SOC_*): each requires more than a hundred options, and each is required by more than sixty. A change to any of them reaches many options, and a change to any of their many requirements can break them: they are the places of the kernel where a careless edit costs most.

Why it matters. A feature that both is needed by many and needs many sits at a crossing: an error in it spreads to its dependants, and a change in any of its requirements reaches it. In a product line those are the features where a careless edit costs most, which deserve the first reviews, the most tests and the most careful evolution.

Limits: what this cannot tell you

“Top tenth” is relative to the model: every model has a warning zone, however healthy. Compare its size between models or versions rather than read it alone. The counts behind it are those of the requires graph.

Layers and hierarchy

This section is about the shape of the requires graph: how its features are layered, from those that need nothing to those that need long chains of others. That shape has a name in mathematics, a partial order Davey and Priestley (2002), and a few classic results about partial orders answer practical questions about variability models. You need none of the theory to use the functions, but the idea is simple, and it explains why the functions work.

What a partial order is, on the band

An order is a way of saying that one thing comes before another, like the numbers 1 < 2 < 3. “ff requires gg” can be read the same way: gg comes before ff, because gg must be there for ff to be there. Three properties make “requires” an order. Each one can be checked on the band:

band$requires |> filter(from == "MovementFilter")
#> # A tibble: 4 x 2
#>   from           to            
#>   <chr>          <chr>         
#> 1 MovementFilter Screen        
#> 2 MovementFilter OLED          
#> 3 MovementFilter CapacityButton
#> 4 MovementFilter BLEv40
band$requires |>
  filter(from %in% c("Screen", "OLED"), to %in% c("Screen", "OLED"))
#> # A tibble: 2 x 2
#>   from   to    
#>   <chr>  <chr> 
#> 1 Screen OLED  
#> 2 OLED   Screen
vp_pair(band, "TouchScreen", "BT40") |> select(combination, possible)
#> # A tibble: 4 x 2
#>   combination      possible
#>   <chr>            <lgl>   
#> 1 both             FALSE   
#> 2 only TouchScreen TRUE    
#> 3 only BT40        TRUE    
#> 4 neither          TRUE

  1. It chains (transitivity). If ff requires gg and gg requires hh, then ff requires hh. MovementFilter requires BLEv40, which requires the screen, and indeed the first table has the arrow from MovementFilter to Screen. variplex’s requires graph always holds every such arrow (it is complete).

  2. It never goes round in a circle (antisymmetry), once an atomic set counts as one feature. The second table shows that the screen requires the OLED panel and the OLED panel requires the screen: they go round in a circle. But two features that require each other are always selected together, so for every choice they are one feature, an atomic set (Atomic sets). Merge each atomic set into one node, and no circle is left: if ff requires gg, then gg does not require ff.

  3. Every feature “requires” itself (reflexivity): trivially, a product with ff has ff. It is a convention that makes the mathematics tidy; the graphs do not draw these arrows.

Why partial? Because in the order of the numbers, of any two numbers one comes before the other: the order is total, a single line. In a partial order, two features can be incomparable: neither requires the other. The last table shows that TouchScreen and BT40 are such a pair: there are bands with only one of them, so neither requires the other (in fact they cannot go together, but a conflict is not a requirement). Of the 36 pairs of the 9 nodes of the band (its atomic set counted once), only 7 are comparable; the other 29 are not.

The skeleton of the Mi Band 3, which draws its partial order: a feature is below the features it requires, and one feature comes before another when a chain of arrows leads from the second to the first. MovementFilter comes after BLEv40 and after the screen; TouchScreen and BT40 (yellow), with no chain between them, are incomparable.

So a partial order is drawn not as a line but as a set of layers with arrows between them: the skeleton (the figure), which keeps only the arrows between immediate neighbours (in the theory of orders it is called the Hasse diagram). Everything in this section is a question about that drawing:

Question about the drawing Function, and the result of order theory behind it
Which features are one node? vp_atomic_sets(): the features that go round in a circle.
Which arrows are between immediate neighbours? vp_skeleton(): the Hasse diagram (transitive reduction Aho et al. (1972)).
In which layer is each feature, and how many layers are there? vp_levels(), vp_depth(): the length of the longest chain (Mirsky’s theorem Mirsky (1971), A safe order for the questions).
How many features are pairwise incomparable, at most? vp_width(): the largest antichain, equal to the fewest chains that cover all the features (Dilworth’s theorem Dilworth (1950)).
Which features are at the top and at the bottom? vp_foundations(), vp_leaves(): the maximal and minimal elements.
What comes with a feature, and what depends on it? vp_upset(), vp_downset(): the up-set and the down-set of the feature.
And with the conflicts too? vp_largest_free_set() and vp_longest_decision_chain(): the counterparts of the width and the depth with the three graphs (Width and chains and Levels, depth and the longest chain).

Atomic sets

Function: vp_atomic_sets()

The question. Which features are really one single decision?

An atomic set is a group of features that require each other, so a product has all of them or none Benavides et al. (2010); Heß and Molt (2025):

vp_atomic_sets(band)
#> # A tibble: 3 x 3
#>     set feature        representative
#>   <int> <chr>          <chr>         
#> 1     1 Screen         Screen        
#> 2     1 OLED           Screen        
#> 3     1 CapacityButton Screen

Screen, OLED and CapacityButton are one decision. The first, Screen, is the representative: it stands for the set in the skeleton and in the other functions of this section. The sets come from the file __atomic.txt, or are computed from the requires graph when there is no such file.

Why it matters. An atomic set is one decision disguised as several features. For a configurator it means one question instead of several; for testing, one value to vary instead of several; for every analysis of the vignettes, one node. Large atomic sets also hint at features that could be merged, or at constraints written so tightly that options can no longer be chosen apart.

Limits: what this cannot tell you

Exact: every group of features that are always selected together is found, and nothing else. But the atomic sets are about features that are selected together; features that are always opposite (one exactly when the other is not, like Screen and BT40) are no atomic set. vp_pair() (Everything about two features) finds them.

The skeleton

Function: vp_skeleton()

The question. Which dependencies carry information, and which ones follow from others?

The requires graph is complete (property P1, Three properties of the graphs). The skeleton keeps only the arrows that do not follow from a chain of others (the transitive reduction Aho et al. (1972)), with each atomic set as one feature:

vp_skeleton(band)
#> # A tibble: 6 x 2
#>   from               to             
#>   <chr>              <chr>          
#> 1 TouchScreen        Screen         
#> 2 ContactlessPayment NFC            
#> 3 MovementFilter     BLEv40         
#> 4 BLEv40             Screen         
#> 5 BLEv42             Screen         
#> 6 BLEv42             HeartRateSensor
vp_implied_requires(band)
#> # A tibble: 1 x 3
#>   from           to     via   
#>   <chr>          <chr>  <chr> 
#> 1 MovementFilter Screen BLEv40

Of the 21 arrows, 6 are in the skeleton (the figure). vp_implied_requires() lists the arrows between different features that follow from others, and one feature they pass through: MovementFilter requires Screen via BLEv40. The other arrows that are not in the skeleton are inside the atomic set. The skeleton is the same as the file __requires_skeleton.net of variplex.

The requires graph of the band. The grey arrows follow from the blue ones: the arrow from MovementFilter to the screen follows from the chain through BLEv40, and the arrows inside the dashed box from the atomic set. Only the blue arrows are in the skeleton.

The skeleton is close to what somebody had to write; the complete graph is what everybody has to live with. Compare their sizes and you know how much of the model is implicit (The whole model in numbers).

Why it matters. The skeleton separates the dependencies that someone had to decide from those that merely follow. Its size against the complete graph measures how much of the model is implicit, which is what makes a model hard to understand by reading it one constraint at a time; and its arrows are the ones to look at when a dependency has to be changed.

Limits: what this cannot tell you

The skeleton is not the list of constraints of the model: an arrow of the skeleton can come from a rule over three features (BLEv42 requires HeartRateSensor is in the skeleton, and no constraint says so), and a constraint that the others imply leaves no arrow of its own. “Follows from a chain of arrows” is the only kind of redundancy it removes: an arrow that follows from a conflict and an at-least-one line stays (Why two features exclude each other).

Levels, depth and the longest chain

Function: vp_levels()

The question. How is the model layered? How long can a line of reasoning get?

The level of a feature is the length of the longest chain of requirements that starts from it: level 0 for a feature that needs nothing, level 1 for one that needs only features of level 0, and so on. The depth is the number of features in the longest chain:

vp_levels(band) |> arrange(level)
#> # A tibble: 11 x 2
#>    feature            level
#>    <chr>              <int>
#>  1 Screen                 0
#>  2 OLED                   0
#>  3 CapacityButton         0
#>  4 HeartRateSensor        0
#>  5 BT40                   0
#>  6 NFC                    0
#>  7 TouchScreen            1
#>  8 ContactlessPayment     1
#>  9 BLEv40                 1
#> 10 BLEv42                 1
#> 11 MovementFilter         2
vp_depth(band)
#> [1] 3
vp_longest_chain(band)
#> # A tibble: 3 x 2
#>    step feature       
#>   <int> <chr>         
#> 1     1 MovementFilter
#> 2     2 BLEv40        
#> 3     3 Screen

The band has three layers. MovementFilter is alone at the top: it requires BLEv40, which requires Screen. That is the longest chain, with three features. The figure draws the skeleton in its levels.

).](figures/am_levels.svg){#fig:levels}

Why it matters. The depth is the longest line of reasoning a user, a developer or a configurator has to follow to see why a feature is forced: a model of depth 17, like Linux, can force an option through 15 intermediate ones. Deep models are harder to explain, to configure step by step (the safe order of A safe order for the questions needs one round per level) and to change, because an edit at the bottom reaches everything above. Depth plays the role of the depth of a feature tree, but it follows the meaning, so it exists for any model, Kconfig included.

Limits: what this cannot tell you

A chain is made of arrows, so a rule over three features that would lengthen a chain (“A needs B or C, and both B and C need D” does make A need D, and the graph has that arrow) counts only through the arrows it implies. Depth also depends on how the model was translated into a formula: two translators of the same Kconfig model can give different depths.

So depth is a warning flag, not a verdict: a large depth says “long explanations live here, look closer”. It sees only arrows of the requires graph, while a conflict can force a decision just as well. The next paragraphs show how to look closer.

After the flag: chains with conflicts too. A requirement “A requires B” is one way a decision forces another. There are three more, all in the graphs: a conflict (“A excludes B”: selecting A forces leaving B out), an at-least-one line (“A or B”: leaving A out forces selecting B), and the contrapositive of each (leaving B out forces leaving A out). vp_mig(), the modal implication graph (The modal implication graph (MIG)), puts them all in one graph whose nodes are decisions: “A” (A selected) and “not A” (A left out). vp_longest_decision_chain() finds the longest line of decisions in it, each forcing the next. Decisions that force each other (opposites, atomic sets) are one step, written together with “=”:

vp_longest_decision_chain(band)
#> # A tibble: 3 x 2
#>    step decisions                                        
#>   <int> <chr>                                            
#> 1     1 BT40 = not CapacityButton = not OLED = not Screen
#> 2     2 not BLEv40                                       
#> 3     3 not MovementFilter
vp_longest_decision_chain(history$model[[7]]) # the Mi Band 8
#> # A tibble: 7 x 2
#>    step decisions                                                             
#>   <int> <chr>                                                                 
#> 1     1 BLEv52                                                                
#> 2     2 SpO2                                                                  
#> 3     3 Photoplethysmogram                                                    
#> 4     4 AMOLED = CapacitivitySensing = FullColor = Gyroscope = ProximitySensor
#> 5     5 not CapacityButton = not OLED                                         
#> 6     6 not BLEv40                                                            
#> 7     7 not MovementFilter
vp_depth(history$model[[7]])
#> [1] 6

On the band the length is the same as the depth, 3, but the chain is another one, and it goes through a conflict: a band without a screen has the classic Bluetooth (BT40), which excludes BLEv40, and without BLEv40 there is no movement filter. Depth, which reads only arrows of the requires graph, sees “MovementFilter requires BLEv40 requires Screen” and nothing else.

On the Mi Band 8 the chain of decisions is longer than the depth: 7 steps against 6. Selecting Bluetooth 5.2 forces SpO2, which forces the photoplethysmogram, which forces the AMOLED screen and its four companions; so far, requirements. Then a conflict: AMOLED and OLED are alternatives, so OLED and its capacity button are left out, and with them BLEv40 and the movement filter. Two of the seven steps are invisible to the depth.

Model Depth Longest chain of decisions What the extra steps are
Mi Band 3 3 3 none, but another chain, through a conflict
Mi Band 8 6 7 a conflict between the screen types
Linux 3.13 17 17 none

What is still missing. The chain of decisions is built from pairs too. A decision that is forced only by two decisions together (“A and B together exclude C”, a rule over three features) is in no graph, and a chain that needs it is not found. When the chain matters (for example, to bound the number of questions a configurator may have to explain), the last check is the formula itself: take the first decision of the chain, give it to a SAT solver as an assumption, and let the solver propagate (on the DIMACS file that vp_generate() keeps with keep_dimacs = TRUE); what it forces is the whole consequence, rules over three features included. Measures that count by pairs, depth and chain alike, can only be shorter than that.

Width and chains

Function: vp_width()

The question. How many decisions are independent of one another, as far as dependencies go?

Depth measures how tall the hierarchy is: the longest line of features each requiring the next. Width measures how broad it is. Call two features related when one requires the other, directly or through a chain. A set of features is unrelated when no two of its features are related: none of them, if selected, forces another one of the set. The width is the size of the largest unrelated set.

vp_width(band)
#> [1] 5
vp_largest_unrelated_set(band)
#> # A tibble: 5 x 1
#>   feature        
#>   <chr>          
#> 1 TouchScreen    
#> 2 HeartRateSensor
#> 3 BLEv40         
#> 4 BT40           
#> 5 NFC
vp_chains(band)
#> # A tibble: 9 x 3
#>   chain position feature           
#>   <int>    <int> <chr>             
#> 1     1        1 TouchScreen       
#> 2     1        2 Screen            
#> 3     2        1 ContactlessPayment
#> 4     2        2 NFC               
#> 5     3        1 MovementFilter    
#> 6     3        2 BLEv40            
#> 7     4        1 BLEv42            
#> 8     4        2 HeartRateSensor   
#> 9     5        1 BT40

The largest unrelated set of the band has five features: TouchScreen, HeartRateSensor, BLEv40, BT40 and NFC (shaded in the figure). Check any pair: the touch screen requires only the screen, BLEv40 only the screen, the three others nothing, so no feature of the set requires another one of the set.

Why no sixth feature fits. vp_chains() splits the nine nodes of the skeleton (the atomic set is one) into chains: lists in which each feature requires the next. Two features of the same chain are always related, so an unrelated set can take at most one feature from each chain. There are five chains, so no unrelated set has more than five features:

Chain Its features In the unrelated set
1 TouchScreen → screen TouchScreen
2 ContactlessPayment → NFC NFC
3 MovementFilter → BLEv40 BLEv40
4 BLEv42 → HeartRateSensor HeartRateSensor
5 BT40 BT40

The unrelated set of five shows that the width is at least 5; the five chains show that it is at most 5. Dilworth’s theorem says that this always happens: the largest unrelated set and the fewest chains that cover all the features have the same size Dilworth (1950). So the two outputs prove each other, and the width is exactly 5.

What it tells. The width is the number of decisions that dependencies leave independent of one another: a configurator can show the five features of the set side by side, and no answer about one of them forces an answer about another (as far as requirements go). A width close to the number of features means a flat model, a long list of independent choices; a small width means a model organised in a few long lines, each a chain of specialisations from a basic feature to its most demanding variants.

Depth and width together describe the shape of a model. A model of nn features always has n≤depth×widthn \le \text{depth} \times \text{width}, so a large model cannot be both shallow and narrow. Shallow and wide means many independent decisions, each easy to explain; deep and narrow, few decisions with long chains of consequences. The band, with depth 3 and width 5 for 9 nodes, is shallow and wide; so is BusyBox (depth 4, width 427 for 623 features); Linux 3.13 is deep and wide (depth 17, width 4,843).

Limits: what this cannot tell you

Width looks only at dependencies. Two features that count as unrelated may still exclude each other, or be tied by a rule over three features: “independent” here means “neither requires the other”, not “free to combine”.

So width is a warning flag, an upper bound: the number of truly free decisions is at most the width, and may be much less. The next paragraphs show how to bring conflicts and at-least-one lines in.

After the flag: free, not just unrelated. Call two features free when the four combinations (both, only the first, only the second, neither) all occur in valid products: then no graph links them, neither requires, excludes nor at-least-one. A set is free when every two of its features are. vp_largest_free_set() finds the largest one, with the three graphs:

vp_largest_free_set(band)
#> # A tibble: 4 x 1
#>   feature           
#>   <chr>             
#> 1 TouchScreen       
#> 2 ContactlessPayment
#> 3 HeartRateSensor   
#> 4 BLEv40
nrow(vp_largest_free_set(history$model[[7]])) # the Mi Band 8
#> [1] 3
vp_width(history$model[[7]])
#> [1] 7

The band has four free features against a width of five. (Do not confuse it with the largest compatible set of Conflicts, vp_largest_compatible_set(): compatible features only need to go together, free features must also be able to go apart, in every combination.) BT40 is gone from the set: it is unrelated to BLEv40 (neither requires the other), but the two exclude each other, since a band has one kind of Bluetooth. (NFC is replaced by ContactlessPayment: the two are in the same chain, so either one fits.) On the Mi Band 8 the gap is wide: width 7, but only 3 free features. The Bluetooth versions are unrelated, which makes the width large, and they are alternatives, which makes them anything but free.

Model Width Largest free set Why they differ
Mi Band 3 5 4 BT40 excludes BLEv40
Mi Band 8 7 3 the Bluetooth versions are alternatives
Linux 3.13 4,843 at least 4,397 conflicts (search not exact at this size)

The third level: free in pairs is not free together. Every two features of a free set take their four combinations; that does not mean the whole set takes its 2k2^k combinations. A rule over three features can forbid one. With the 24 products of the band (the table products of Measuring each feature) the check is a count:

free <- vp_largest_free_set(band)$feature
products |> count(across(all_of(free)))
#>    TouchScreen ContactlessPayment HeartRateSensor BLEv40 n
#> 1            0                  0               0      0 2
#> 2            0                  0               0      1 2
#> 3            0                  0               1      0 4
#> 4            0                  0               1      1 2
#> 5            0                  1               0      0 1
#> 6            0                  1               0      1 1
#> 7            0                  1               1      0 2
#> 8            0                  1               1      1 1
#> 9            1                  0               0      1 2
#> 10           1                  0               1      0 2
#> 11           1                  0               1      1 2
#> 12           1                  1               0      1 1
#> 13           1                  1               1      0 1
#> 14           1                  1               1      1 1

Fourteen of the sixteen combinations occur. The two missing ones are a touch screen with neither the heart-rate sensor nor BLEv40. A band with a screen cannot have the classic Bluetooth, so it has BLE, and the model says “BLE needs the heart-rate sensor or the movement filter”; the movement filter needs BLEv40. So a touch screen needs the sensor or BLEv40: a rule over three features that no pair shows. So, of the four free features, a configurator can offer any two side by side, but not all four as independent switches.

When the products cannot be listed, the same question goes to the formula: one call of a SAT solver per combination (2k2^k calls, with each combination given as assumptions), or one call of a model counter such as GANAK per combination, which also says how many products have it. For kk up to about 15 this is quick. It is the only exact answer: the graphs can flag the problem, and the formula settles it.

Limits: what this cannot tell you

vp_largest_free_set() solves a hard problem (a largest independent set). Up to 60 variable features (exact_limit) the search is exact; above it, a greedy search gives a free set that cannot be extended, and the largest one may be larger: on Linux the answer is a lower bound. It is also about pairs, and the third level above is what it cannot see.

How it works inside

The width comes from a maximum matching in a graph with two copies of each feature, one as “requires” and one as “is required” (igraph::max_bipartite_match()): each matched pair is a link of a chain, so the chains are the features minus the matched pairs. König’s theorem turns the same matching into a largest set of unrelated features. The depth comes from one pass over the features in topological order. Both are fast on Linux.

Foundations and leaves

Function: vp_foundations()

The question. Which features are the base of everything, and which ones could be removed without breaking anything?

vp_foundations(band)
#> # A tibble: 4 x 1
#>   feature        
#>   <chr>          
#> 1 Screen         
#> 2 HeartRateSensor
#> 3 BT40           
#> 4 NFC
vp_leaves(band)
#> # A tibble: 5 x 1
#>   feature           
#>   <chr>             
#> 1 TouchScreen       
#> 2 ContactlessPayment
#> 3 MovementFilter    
#> 4 BLEv42            
#> 5 BT40

Foundations need nothing: every chain of requirements ends in one of them. Leaves are needed by nothing: removing one breaks no other feature. Some features are both, like BT40: in the skeleton they stand alone.

Why it matters. Foundations are where the product line starts: the features every chain of requirements ends in, which must be designed, tested and kept stable first. Leaves are where it ends: features nothing depends on, which can be removed or changed without breaking another feature, and where new features are usually attached. The two lists are the two ends of a refactoring or a clean-up.

Limits: what this cannot tell you

“Removing a leaf breaks no other feature” is true of the requires graph. A rule over three features (“A needs B or C”) can still lean on a leaf: remove C, and A needs B.

What a selection drags in, and what depends on it

Function: vp_upset()

The question. If I select these features, what else comes with them? If I change this feature, what is affected?

The up-set of some features is themselves and everything they require; the down-set is themselves and everything that requires one of them. vp_upset() says which given feature brings each one; vp_downset() which given feature each one depends on:

vp_upset(band, c("MovementFilter", "NFC"))
#> # A tibble: 6 x 2
#>   feature        brought_by    
#>   <chr>          <chr>         
#> 1 MovementFilter MovementFilter
#> 2 NFC            NFC           
#> 3 Screen         MovementFilter
#> 4 OLED           MovementFilter
#> 5 CapacityButton MovementFilter
#> 6 BLEv40         MovementFilter
vp_downset(band, "BLEv40")
#> # A tibble: 2 x 2
#>   feature        depends_on
#>   <chr>          <chr>     
#> 1 BLEv40         BLEv40    
#> 2 MovementFilter BLEv40

The figure shows the up-set of the two features on the skeleton. Two more functions find where two features meet: vp_common_requirements(band, a, b) (what both need: shared infrastructure) and vp_common_dependants(band, a, b) (what needs both: where two parts of the model are tied together):

vp_common_requirements(band, "MovementFilter", "BLEv42")
#> # A tibble: 3 x 1
#>   feature       
#>   <chr>         
#> 1 Screen        
#> 2 OLED          
#> 3 CapacityButton
vp_common_dependants(band, "Screen", "HeartRateSensor")
#> # A tibble: 1 x 1
#>   feature
#>   <chr>  
#> 1 BLEv42

The movement filter and Bluetooth 4.2 share the screen and its atomic set (the figure); nothing requires both the screen and the heart-rate sensor except BLEv42.

The up-set of MovementFilter and NFC (yellow): the features they bring along, in green, are those reached by following the arrows upwards.
The common requirements of MovementFilter and BLEv42 (yellow): the screen and its atomic set (green), which both reach by following the arrows.

Why it matters. The up-set is what a customer really gets when choosing some features, and what a product will contain whether or not anyone asked for it; the down-set is everything a change to a feature can affect. Both are what impact analysis and configuration explanations are built on.

Limits: what this cannot tell you

The up-set is what selecting the features forces through requirements. It is not everything a selection settles: it leaves out what the features exclude (see vp_consequences(), What some decisions force), and, through rules over three or more features, two selections together can force a feature that neither forces alone.

A feature tree rebuilt from the graphs

Function: vp_feature_tree()

The question. What feature tree do the dependencies suggest? Useful for Kconfig, which has no tree, and to compare with the tree of a UVL model.

Each feature gets as parent one of the features it requires directly in the skeleton. When there are several candidates, the least required one is chosen (the simplest of the rules studied in the work on feature-model synthesis Czarnecki and Wąsowski (2007); She et al. (2011); Andersen et al. (2012)), and the others become cross-tree requirements:

vp_feature_tree(band)
#> # A tibble: 9 x 4
#>   feature            parent          candidates cross_tree
#>   <chr>              <chr>                <int> <chr>     
#> 1 Screen             <NA>                     0 ""        
#> 2 TouchScreen        Screen                   1 ""        
#> 3 ContactlessPayment NFC                      1 ""        
#> 4 MovementFilter     BLEv40                   1 ""        
#> 5 HeartRateSensor    <NA>                     0 ""        
#> 6 BLEv40             Screen                   1 ""        
#> 7 BLEv42             HeartRateSensor          2 "Screen"  
#> 8 BT40               <NA>                     0 ""        
#> 9 NFC                <NA>                     0 ""
The tree that the skeleton of the band suggests: black lines join a feature (below) to the parent chosen for it (above). The dashed blue arrow is a requirement that the tree cannot hold: BLEv42 needs the screen too.

Compare with the figure. BLEv42 hangs from HeartRateSensor instead of from BLE, which is abstract and so not in the graphs, and the screen becomes a cross-tree requirement. Screen, HeartRateSensor, BT40 and NFC need nothing, so they have no parent (NA): they are the tops of the tree, where a feature model would hang them from its root.

Models without a tree. vp_feature_tree() reads only the graphs, never the file the model came from, so it works on every model variplex accepts: UVL, a DIMACS formula of any origin, or Kconfig (through its DIMACS translation). The last two have no feature tree at all, and that is where the function is most useful. BusyBox is a Kconfig model; the package has only its graphs, from the published dataset (The examples), not its Kconfig files nor its formula, and that is enough:

tree_bb <- vp_feature_tree(bb)
c(
  features = nrow(tree_bb),
  tops = sum(is.na(tree_bb$parent)),
  one_candidate = sum(tree_bb$candidates == 1),
  with_cross_tree = sum(tree_bb$cross_tree != "")
)
#>        features            tops   one_candidate with_cross_tree 
#>             602             177             375              50
tree_bb |> count(parent, sort = TRUE) |> filter(!is.na(parent)) |> head(3)
#> # A tibble: 3 x 2
#>   parent              n
#>   <chr>           <int>
#> 1 CONFIG_FIND        20
#> 2 CONFIG_VOLUMEID    19
#> 3 CONFIG_ASH         13
tree_bb |> filter(parent == "CONFIG_FIND") |> select(feature, parent) |> head(4)
#> # A tibble: 4 x 2
#>   feature                      parent     
#>   <chr>                        <chr>      
#> 1 CONFIG_FEATURE_FIND_PRUNE    CONFIG_FIND
#> 2 CONFIG_FEATURE_FIND_XDEV     CONFIG_FIND
#> 3 CONFIG_FEATURE_FIND_MTIME    CONFIG_FIND
#> 4 CONFIG_FEATURE_FIND_MAXDEPTH CONFIG_FIND

The rebuilt tree gives BusyBox a shape from its graphs alone: each applet (find, ash, hush) becomes a parent, with its options as children. find alone has twenty: -prune, -xdev, -mtime and the rest. For the features with one candidate (375 of 602) there is only one possible parent, so for them the tree is not a guess. The 177 tops, features that need nothing, would hang from the root of a feature model, and 50 features keep a cross-tree requirement.

For a model without a tree, this is a first feature diagram, to read the model or to start a UVL version of it. Whether the tree agrees with the menus of the Kconfig files is a separate question, which needs those files.

Using the rebuilt tree to refactor a model. A refactoring changes how a model is written and keeps its products: the same valid configurations, before and after Thüm et al. (2009). A common reason to refactor is to turn cross-tree constraints into tree edges. A constraint “A requires B” says, in the margin, what the tree could say by hanging A under B. Fewer constraints make a model easier to read, and the tree carries the meaning where the reader looks first.

The rebuilt tree is a list of such proposals. Every parent it chooses is a true requirement of the child, so hanging the child there never loses a product. The Mi Band 8 has 22 constraint lines. Its rebuilt tree and its graphs suggest three of them can go:

tree8_rebuilt <- vp_feature_tree(history$model[[7]])
tree8_rebuilt |> filter(feature %in% c("SpO2", "ContactlessPayment"))
#> # A tibble: 2 x 4
#>   feature            parent             candidates cross_tree
#>   <chr>              <chr>                   <int> <chr>     
#> 1 ContactlessPayment TouchScreen                 1 ""        
#> 2 SpO2               Photoplethysmogram          1 ""
vp_atomic_sets(history$model[[7]]) |>
  filter(feature %in% c("NFC", "ContactlessPayment"))
#> # A tibble: 2 x 3
#>     set feature            representative    
#>   <int> <chr>              <chr>             
#> 1     3 ContactlessPayment ContactlessPayment
#> 2     3 NFC                ContactlessPayment

  • SpO2 hangs from Sensors in the model and needs the photoplethysmogram through the constraint SpO2 => Photoplethysmogram. The rebuilt tree puts it under Photoplethysmogram. Move it there as an optional child, and the constraint goes.

  • NFC and ContactlessPayment are an atomic set: two constraints say that each requires the other. Make NFC a mandatory child of ContactlessPayment, and both constraints go.

The changes, from the realized model to the refactored one:

Where Before After
NFC optional child of Connectivity mandatory child of ContactlessPayment
SpO2 optional child of Sensors optional child of Photoplethysmogram
Constraints NFC => ContactlessPayment deleted
ContactlessPayment => NFC deleted
SpO2 => Photoplethysmogram deleted

Check that it is a refactoring. Run variplex on both models (the new one is vp_example("miband8_refactored.uvl")), with representativeness = TRUE so that it counts the products (this needs the model counter GANAK), and compare. Identical graphs and the same number of products are two necessary conditions:

before <- vp_generate(
  vp_example("miband8_realized.uvl"),
  or_graph = TRUE,
  representativeness = TRUE
)
after <- vp_generate(
  vp_example("miband8_refactored.uvl"),
  or_graph = TRUE,
  representativeness = TRUE
)
vp_compare(before, after) |>
  select(graph, added, removed, gained, lost, jaccard)
#> # A tibble: 3 x 6
#>   graph      added removed gained  lost jaccard
#>   <chr>      <int>   <int>  <int> <int>   <dbl>
#> 1 requires       0       0      0     0       1
#> 2 excludes       0       0      0     0       1
#> 3 atleastone     0       0      0     0       1
c(
  before = vp_representativeness(before)$vm_configurations,
  after = vp_representativeness(after)$vm_configurations
)
#> before  after 
#>     21     21

No feature added or removed, no link gained or lost, 21 products before and after. Neither condition alone proves the refactoring: two formulas can have the same graphs and differ in a rule over three features, and two formulas can have the same number of products and different products. The proof is that each formula implies the other, which a SAT solver checks in two calls Thüm et al. (2009). For this small model the 21 products of each version were listed and compared for the vignettes: they are the same.

Where not to follow the tree. The rebuilt tree also hangs the photoplethysmogram under the AMOLED screen, and the gyroscope and the proximity sensor are in the atomic set of the AMOLED screen, so the graphs would make them mandatory children of the screen. Both moves keep the products, and both remove constraints. Both are bad trees: a sensor is not a part of a screen. The constraints say a business fact (the premium screen comes with premium sensors), not a part-of relation, and a tree that hides that fact behind a part-of edge misleads the reader. The graphs propose by meaning; the designer decides by the domain.

Why it matters. Feature models are read through their trees, and models from Kconfig or plain formulas have none. A tree rebuilt from the meaning gives such models a first diagram, and for UVL models it is a second opinion on the declared tree: where the two disagree, either the tree hides a layer or a refactoring is possible.

Limits: what this cannot tell you

  • A tree is a proposal, not a discovery. The graphs give each feature its candidate parents; the choice among them is a rule of thumb. The rebuilt tree finds where a feature can hang without losing products; it does not say where it should.

  • Groups of the model (“exactly one of these children”) are rules over many features, so the rebuilt tree has no groups: the alternatives appear as conflicts between siblings. Abstract features, left out of the graphs, cannot become parents. Both have to be added by hand.

  • A refactoring must be proved on the formula, as above: the graphs are evidence, not proof.

Operations that need the feature tree

The next three operations need the tree of the model, read with vp_read_uvl_tree(). Do not confuse it with vp_feature_tree(): they have similar names and answer opposite questions.

vp_read_uvl_tree(file) vp_feature_tree(model)
Reads the UVL file, as written by its designer the graphs that variplex computed
Answers “what tree did the designer draw?” “what tree does the meaning suggest?”
Features all of them: abstract, core and dead too only those in the graphs (variable, concrete)
Kinds of child mandatory, optional, alternative, or none: every parent is a requirement;
(the relation column) the rest goes to cross_tree
Works on Kconfig no (Kconfig has no UVL tree) yes
Is it the truth? it is the model, whatever it means a proposal: a rule of thumb picks the parent

vp_read_uvl_tree() does not look at the graphs at all, and vp_feature_tree() does not look at the UVL file. The operations of this subsection put the two side by side: the drawing of the model against what its constraints mean.

False-optional features

Function: vp_false_optional()

The question. Which features are declared optional and are not?

A classic analysis of feature models Benavides et al. (2010). Two definitions are in use: an optional feature is false-optional when it is in every product, or, the definition that Nieke et al. consider more sensible Nieke et al. (2018), when it is selected whenever its parent is. The graphs decide both: the first is the list of core features, the second an arrow from the parent to the child. uClibc, one of the examples of variplex, has both kinds:

uclibc <- vp_read("uclibc/uClibc")
tree_u <- vp_read_uvl_tree("data/uClibc.uvl")
vp_false_optional(uclibc, tree_u)
#> # A tibble: 6 x 4
#>   feature                      parent                in_every_product whenever_parent
#>   <chr>                        <chr>                 <lgl>            <lgl>          
#> 1 ARCH_HAS_NO_SHARED           root                  TRUE             TRUE           
#> 2 UCLIBC_HAS_LOCALE            root                  TRUE             TRUE           
#> 3 ARCH_HAS_NO_LDSO             root                  TRUE             TRUE           
#> 4 UCLIBC_UCLINUX_BROKEN_MUNMAP root                  TRUE             TRUE           
#> 5 UCLIBC_HAS_CRYPT             UCLIBC_HAS_CRYPT_IMPL FALSE            TRUE           
#> 6 UCLIBC_HAS_FPU               UCLIBC_HAS_FLOATS     FALSE            TRUE

The rows with in_every_product TRUE are core: every product has them, although the tree says they are optional. The others are selected in every product that has their parent: a C library with crypt support always has the crypt implementation, and one with floating point always has the option of the FPU.

Why it matters. A false-optional feature is a defect of a feature model in the classic catalogue: the tree promises a choice that the constraints take away. Users are offered an option that is not one, documentation describes variability that does not exist, and tests may be planned for configurations that cannot be built.

Limits: what this cannot tell you

Exact for both definitions, when the parent is in the graphs. When the parent is abstract (left out of the graphs), the second definition cannot be checked and whenever_parent is NA; run vp_generate() with abstract = "keep" to keep the abstract features.

Does the tree hide layers?

Function: vp_tree_agreement()

The question. Is each feature’s declared parent its immediate requirement, or do other features stand in between?

In a feature tree a child requires its parent. When the child reaches its parent only through other features (it requires something that requires the parent), the tree hides a layer of the hierarchy: a “hierarchy violation” in the sense of Berger and Guo Berger and Guo (2014), measured by meaning. The Mi Band 8 has one:

band8 <- history$model[[7]]
tree8 <- vp_read_uvl_tree("data/miband8_realized.uvl")
vp_tree_agreement(band8, tree8)
#> # A tibble: 3 x 4
#>   feature            parent          direct in_between           
#>   <chr>              <chr>           <lgl>  <chr>                
#> 1 TouchScreen        Screen          TRUE   ""                   
#> 2 FullColor          TouchScreen     TRUE   ""
