#> 3 Photoplethysmogram HeartRateSensor FALSE  "AMOLED, TouchScreen"

The tree puts the photoplethysmogram sensor under the heart-rate sensor (the figure), but the constraints make it need the AMOLED screen, which needs the touch screen, which needs the heart-rate sensor. The share of FALSE rows measures how far the drawing of a model is from its meaning.

Why it matters. People read a feature model by its tree, so a hidden layer is a hidden cost, and each FALSE row is worth a look for one of these reasons:

  • The reader is misled. The tree shows the photoplethysmogram as a small option of the heart-rate sensor. In fact, selecting it brings in the AMOLED screen, the touch screen, a Bluetooth 5 version, the gyroscope and the proximity sensor. A product manager who prices the option by the tree prices it wrong.

  • The configurator asks in the wrong order. A configurator that follows the tree asks about the heart-rate sensor, then about the photoplethysmogram, and only later about the screen. A user who says yes to the photoplethysmogram then finds the screen already decided, or, if the screen was asked first and refused, finds the option disabled for no visible reason. The safe order of A safe order for the questions asks about the screen first.

  • It may be a bug. Either the tree is out of date (the feature has moved in the product, and the drawing has not followed: a refactoring candidate, see vp_feature_tree()), or a constraint is stronger than intended. Here the constraint is Photoplethysmogram => BLEv50 | BLEv52 | BLEv51, about Bluetooth. It drags in the screen only because another constraint ties those Bluetooth versions to the AMOLED screen. That is probably a fact of the product line, but it is worth a question to its designer.

  • It tracks drift. Across versions, a growing share of FALSE rows means the drawing and the meaning are drifting apart, the erosion that Berger and Guo measured in real models Berger and Guo (2014).

Mi Band 8. The tree (dashed line) makes the photoplethysmogram sensor a child of the heart-rate sensor; the skeleton (blue arrows) shows two layers in between.

Limits: what this cannot tell you

Only pairs whose child and parent are both in the graphs are compared: abstract parents, and core ones, are left out. The comparison is with the skeleton, so it inherits its limit: a rule over three features does not appear as a layer.

Candidate redundant constraints

Function: vp_redundant_candidates()

The question. Which constraints of the model say nothing new, and could be deleted without changing its products?

What a redundant constraint is. Suppose a model says “the movement filter requires BLE 4.0” and “BLE 4.0 requires the screen”. If someone also writes “the movement filter requires the screen”, that third constraint is redundant: it follows from the other two, so deleting it leaves exactly the same products. Redundant constraints are common in models that many people edit over the years. They do no harm to the products, but they make the model longer to read, and they mislead: whoever later changes “BLE 4.0 requires the screen” may not notice that a copy of its consequence is written elsewhere, and may wonder why the movement filter still needs the screen.

The rule. A written requirement “A requires B” is redundant, in this sense, when A reaches B through a chain of other requirements, A →\to X →⋯→\to \cdots \to B. The skeleton (The skeleton) is exactly the set of arrows that no such chain explains. So the test is simple: a written requirement that is not an arrow of the skeleton is redundant; one that is an arrow of the skeleton carries information of its own.

What to give it. The graphs do not know which constraints were written; you tell the function, as a tibble with the columns from and to, one row per written requirement “from requires to”. A first example on the band: five requirements someone might have written, among them the third constraint of the story above, and one that is false:

written_band <- tribble(
  ~from                , ~to      ,
  "MovementFilter"     , "BLEv40" ,
  "MovementFilter"     , "Screen" ,
  "ContactlessPayment" , "NFC"    ,
  "OLED"               , "Screen" ,
  "TouchScreen"        , "BLEv40"
)
vp_redundant_candidates(band, written_band)
#> # A tibble: 5 x 5
#>   from               to     in_graphs redundant via              
#>   <chr>              <chr>  <lgl>     <lgl>     <chr>            
#> 1 MovementFilter     BLEv40 TRUE      FALSE     ""               
#> 2 MovementFilter     Screen TRUE      TRUE      "BLEv40"         
#> 3 ContactlessPayment NFC    TRUE      FALSE     ""               
#> 4 OLED               Screen TRUE      FALSE     "same atomic set"
#> 5 TouchScreen        BLEv40 FALSE     FALSE     ""

Read it with the skeleton of the band in the figure:

Written requirement What the columns say
MovementFilter → BLEv40 in_graphs TRUE: the model implies it. redundant FALSE: it is an arrow of the skeleton, no other chain gives it. Keep it.
MovementFilter → Screen redundant TRUE, via BLEv40: the chain MovementFilter → BLEv40 → screen already gives it. A candidate for deletion.
ContactlessPayment → NFC Not redundant: nothing else makes contactless payment need NFC.
OLED → Screen via “same atomic set”: the two are always selected together, so each requires the other and neither arrow can be removed without changing what the set means. Not a candidate.
TouchScreen → BLEv40 in_graphs FALSE: the model does not imply it (there are bands with a touch screen and BLE 4.2). A written requirement that the graphs do not hold means that the list you gave does not match the model: a typo, a constraint from another version, or a constraint that something else overrides. Worth checking, for the opposite reason.

On a real model. In a UVL model, the written requirements are of two kinds: the edges of the tree (a child requires its parent) and the cross-tree constraints of the form A => B. A constraint such as MovementFilter => !HeartRateSensor & BLEv40 contains one requirement, MovementFilter → BLEv40, and a conflict, which is not a requirement. The Mi Band 8, with the tree edges between features that can vary (core and abstract features are not in the graphs) and three of its constraints:

vars <- vp_features(band8) |> filter(status == "variable") |> pull(feature)
# the tree: a child requires its parent
written <- tree8 |>
  filter(feature %in% vars, parent %in% vars) |>
  select(from = feature, to = parent) |>
  # and three constraints
  bind_rows(tibble(
    from = c("MovementFilter", "SpO2", "BLEv52"),
    to = c("BLEv40", "Photoplethysmogram", "SpO2")
  ))
vp_redundant_candidates(band8, written)
#> # A tibble: 8 x 5
#>   from                to                 in_graphs redundant via              
#>   <chr>               <chr>              <lgl>     <lgl>     <chr>            
#> 1 CapacityButton      OLED               TRUE      FALSE     "same atomic set"
#> 2 CapacitivitySensing AMOLED             TRUE      FALSE     "same atomic set"
#> 3 TouchScreen         Screen             TRUE      FALSE     ""               
#> 4 FullColor           TouchScreen        TRUE      FALSE     ""               
#> 5 Photoplethysmogram  HeartRateSensor    TRUE      TRUE      "AMOLED"         
#> 6 MovementFilter      BLEv40             TRUE      FALSE     ""               
#> 7 SpO2                Photoplethysmogram TRUE      FALSE     ""               
#> 8 BLEv52              SpO2               TRUE      FALSE     ""

One candidate: the tree edge from the photoplethysmogram sensor to the heart-rate sensor, redundant via the AMOLED screen. It is the hidden layer of the previous operation seen from the other side: the constraints already make the sensor need the AMOLED screen, which needs the touch screen, which needs the heart-rate sensor, so the tree edge adds nothing. A tree edge cannot simply be deleted (every feature hangs from somewhere), but it can be moved: hang the photoplethysmogram sensor under the AMOLED screen, as the rebuilt tree suggests (A feature tree rebuilt from the graphs), and the hierarchy says what the constraints mean. The other written requirements carry information of their own, or join features of one atomic set.

Why it matters. A redundant constraint is one more line to read and one more place to update: whoever changes one of the constraints it repeats must find it too, or the model ends up saying two different things. Finding the redundant ones lets a model say each thing once.

Before deleting. Treat each candidate as a proposal and confirm it the way a refactoring is confirmed: delete the constraint, run variplex on both versions and check that the graphs and the number of products are the same, or, for a proof, that each formula implies the other.

Limits: what this cannot tell you

  • “Redundant” here means “implied by a chain of requirements”. A requirement can also follow from a conflict and an at-least-one line (vp_requires_from_conflicts(), Conflicts), or from rules over three features; those stay arrows of the skeleton and are not flagged. So a FALSE in redundant does not prove that the constraint is needed.

  • It only examines requirements between two features: a constraint over three or more features, or a conflict, cannot be given to it.

  • The same requirement written twice (two constraints that say the same) is one arrow of the graphs: give the list without duplicates, and look for duplicates in the text of the model.

  • Removing one redundant constraint can make another one necessary: if A => B, B => C and A => C are written and B => C is later deleted, A => C stops being redundant. Delete one at a time, and check after each.

The whole model in numbers

One row per model

Function: vp_summary()

The question. How does this model compare with others? Has it become more entangled from one version to the next?

vp_summary() sums a model up in one row. Give it several models, with names, and it stacks their rows. The band, the last month of BusyBox and Linux 3.13, side by side (t() turns the table so that each model is a column):

s <- vp_summary(band = band, busybox = bb, linux = linux)
s |> select(-form) |> tibble::column_to_rownames("model") |> t() |> round(3)
#>                             band busybox     linux
#> features                  11.000 623.000  7100.000
#> core                       8.000   8.000   136.000
#> dead                       0.000   0.000  2181.000
#> atomic_sets                1.000  18.000   301.000
#> requires                  21.000 735.000 88018.000
#> excludes                  10.000 131.000 57667.000
#> atleastone                 3.000      NA   899.000
#> skeleton                   6.000 478.000 11403.000
#> primitive_conflicts        3.000  38.000   578.000
#> implicit_requires          0.143   0.186     0.778
#> implicit_excludes          0.625   0.686     0.985
#> density_requires           0.191   0.002     0.002
#> density_excludes           0.182   0.001     0.002
#> depth                      3.000   4.000    17.000
#> width                      5.000 427.000  4843.000
#> cross_tree_share           0.167   0.111     0.444
#> hierarchy_share            0.194   0.003     0.002
#> gini_required_by           0.649   0.850     0.947
#> gini_excludes              0.500   0.927     0.935
#> mean_decision_power        0.373   0.003     0.004
#> isolated                   0.000  38.000     9.000
#> coupling                   1.000   0.939     0.999
#> skeleton_per_feature       0.667   0.794     1.737
#> largest_atomic_set         3.000   3.000    57.000
#> largest_alternative_group  3.000   6.000    26.000
#> representativeness         0.571      NA        NA

The formulas use the notation of Measuring each feature, and three more symbols: V′V', ⇒′\Rightarrow' and #′\#' are the features and links once each atomic set counts as one node, n′=|V′|n' = |V'|; PP is the set of primitive conflicts; and rr the number of nodes of V′V' that require nothing.

Column Formula Meaning
features, core, dead nn, and the sizes of the two lists The features that can vary (the dots), and those in every product or in none.
atomic_sets Atomic sets of two or more features.
requires, excludes, atleastone |⇒||{\Rightarrow}|, |#||{\#}|, |∨||{\vee}| The links of the three graphs.
skeleton, primitive_conflicts |S||S|, |P||P| The links of the minimal form (The skeleton and Primitive conflicts).
implicit_requires 1−|S||⇒′|1 - \dfrac{|S|}{|{\Rightarrow'}|} The share of the dependencies that follow from others.
implicit_excludes 1−|P||#′|1 - \dfrac{|P|}{|{\#'}|} The share of the conflicts that are inherited from a primitive one.
density_requires |⇒|n(n−1)\dfrac{|{\Rightarrow}|}{n(n-1)} Arrows over the possible ones: the chance that a change to a random feature affects another random feature, the propagation cost of MacCormack et al. MacCormack et al. (2006).
density_excludes |#|n(n−1)/2\dfrac{|{\#}|}{n(n-1)/2} Conflicts over the possible ones: the share of pairs that no product has together.
depth 1+max⁡flevel(f)1 + \max_{f} \text{level}(f) The number of features of the longest chain (Levels, depth and the longest chain).
width max⁡|W|\max |W|, over the sets W⊆V′W \subseteq V' with no f⇒gf \Rightarrow g inside The largest set of features none of which requires another (Width and chains).
cross_tree_share 1−n′−r|S|1 - \dfrac{n' - r}{|S|} How far the skeleton is from a tree, which would have one arrow per node that requires something.
hierarchy_share |⇒′|n′(n′−1)/2\dfrac{|{\Rightarrow'}|}{n'(n'-1)/2} The share of pairs related by a requirement: 0 for a flat list of choices, 1 for a single chain.
gini_required_by, gini_excludes ∑i=1n(2i−n−1)x(i)n∑ixi\dfrac{\sum_{i=1}^{n} (2i - n - 1)\, x_{(i)}}{n \sum_{i} x_i}, with x(1)≤…≤x(n)x_{(1)} \le \dots \le x_{(n)} the values sorted How unevenly the dependants (required_by) and the conflicts (excludes) are spread: 0 if every feature has as many, near 1 if one feature has them all (vp_gini()).
mean_decision_power 1n∑f∈Vdecision_power(f)\dfrac{1}{n}\sum_{f \in V} \text{decision\_power}(f) The average share of the model that selecting one feature decides.
isolated |{f∈V:f is isolated}||\{f \in V : f \text{ is isolated}\}| Features in no graph.
coupling 1−isolatedn1 - \dfrac{\text{isolated}}{n} The share of features with at least one strong relationship: the counterpart, by meaning, of the cross-tree constraint ratio of the literature.
skeleton_per_feature |S|n′\dfrac{|S|}{n'} Links of the skeleton per node: density by meaning.
largest_atomic_set max⁡|A|\max |A|, over the atomic sets AA The largest group of mutually dependent features: what Baldwin et al. call the “core” of an architecture Baldwin et al. (2014).
largest_alternative_group max⁡|K|\max |K|, over the sets K⊆VK \subseteq V with f#gf \mathbin{\#} g for all f≠gf \ne g in KK The most features that all exclude one another (Groups of alternatives).

What each number means for a product line.

  • features, core, dead: the real choices of the line, and how many declared options are no choice at all (core options are in every product, dead ones in none: both are worth a look, as false-optional features or left-overs).

  • requires, excludes, atleastone, skeleton, primitive_conflicts: how many relationships users and maintainers live with, and how many were decided.

  • implicit_requires, implicit_excludes: how much of the model nobody wrote. High values mean that reading the constraints one by one shows little of what the model forbids or forces: explanations, impact analysis and tool support are needed.

  • density_requires (propagation cost) and density_excludes: how likely a change to one feature reaches another, and how much of the space of pairs is forbidden. High values mean costly changes and tightly constrained products.

  • depth, width, hierarchy_share, cross_tree_share: the shape of the line. Deep means long explanations and many configuration rounds; wide, many independent choices; a high cross-tree share, a hierarchy far from a tree, which a feature diagram will draw poorly.

  • gini_required_by, gini_excludes: whether a few features carry the dependencies or the conflicts, that is, whether the line rests on a few critical features.

  • mean_decision_power: how fast a configuration session converges. Low values mean that users take most decisions one by one.

  • isolated, coupling: how many options stand alone (free to combine, cheap to test) and how entangled the rest is.

  • skeleton_per_feature: how many decided dependencies each feature carries, a size-free measure of how much was written.

  • largest_atomic_set, largest_alternative_group: the largest block of features that must go together, and the largest choice of “one of these”; the second is also a floor on the products any test campaign must build.

Read across. The three models differ most in how implicit they are and in how much a selection decides:

  • In Linux, 78 % of the dependencies and 98.5 % of the conflicts follow from others: a few 578 primitive conflicts produce 57,667. Nobody can see them by reading one constraint at a time.

  • In BusyBox only 19 % of the dependencies are implicit: its dependencies are short and mostly written.

  • Selecting a feature of the band decides 37 % of the others on average; in BusyBox 0.26 %, in Linux 0.40 %. In a large model each decision settles little, and the user takes most of them one by one.

vp_summary(linux) takes about 7 seconds on a laptop. Every function of the vignettes works at that scale, except those that say otherwise (they try every combination, or build a graph of pairs of features).

Why it matters. One row per model is what makes models and versions comparable: is this product line more entangled than that one, has it become more implicit since last year, does a translator produce models of a different shape?

Limits: what this cannot tell you

  • Every number describes the graphs, not the model: a rule over three or more features changes none of them unless it implies a relationship between two (Limits and theory shows a rule that changes nothing).

  • The numbers depend on what counts as a feature. Graphs that still hold helper variables of a translation (the published dataset of version 1 of Strong4VM, for Kconfig) give very different values; filter them first (Graphs made by version 1 of Strong4VM).

  • The implicit shares say how many relationships follow from others in the graphs; the share of written constraints that are redundant would need the model.

  • largest_alternative_group is computed exactly; on graphs with hundreds of thousands of conflicts this can take long.

Are the files consistent?

Function: vp_check()

The question. Were the files damaged, or filtered by hand in one graph and not in the other?

The graphs of any model have properties that vp_check() verifies: one row per property, with the number of cases that break it.

vp_check(band)
#> # A tibble: 6 x 3
#>   property                                                           holds violations
#>   <chr>                                                              <lgl>      <int>
#> 1 requires is complete: A -> B and B -> C give A -> C                TRUE           0
#> 2 conflicts are inherited: A -> B and B excludes C give A excludes C TRUE           0
#> 3 no feature requires two features that exclude each other           TRUE           0
#> 4 no pair both requires and excludes                                 TRUE           0
#> 5 at-least-one is inherited upwards: A or B, and B -> C give A or C  TRUE           0
#> 6 A excludes B and (B or C) give A -> C                              TRUE           0

Among them are properties P1 and P2 of Three properties of the graphs. A FALSE means that the files are incomplete, and every other measure of the vignettes assumes that they are not. The same checks run at the end of every run of vp_generate(); this function is for graphs you have read from elsewhere, filtered or edited in R.

Why it matters. Every analysis of the vignettes trusts the files. Graphs filtered by hand, merged from several runs, or damaged in transfer can break the properties that the analyses rely on, and give wrong answers without any error. Checking them first is cheap insurance.

Limits: what this cannot tell you

The checks test the files against each other, not against the model. Files that pass them can still come from a model other than the one you think, or miss a relationship that the model implies; only a new run of variplex settles that.

Degree distributions and concentration

Function: vp_degree_distribution()

The question. Do a few features carry most of the dependencies, or are the dependencies spread over many?

Two tools answer it. The degree distribution is the full picture: how many features have each number of dependants. The Gini coefficient sums that picture up in one number, which can be compared between models and followed through versions.

The degree distribution

The degree of a feature, here, is how many features require it: its required_by. vp_degree_distribution() counts how many features have each degree. On the band it is short enough to read whole:

vp_degree_distribution(band, "requires")
#> # A tibble: 3 x 2
#>   degree features
#>    <int>    <int>
#> 1      0        5
#> 2      1        3
#> 3      6        3
vp_degree_distribution(band, "skeleton")
#> # A tibble: 3 x 2
#>   degree features
#>    <int>    <int>
#> 1      0        5
#> 2      1        3
#> 3      3        1

Each row says: features features are required by exactly degree others. In the complete requires graph, 5 features are required by nobody (TouchScreen, ContactlessPayment, MovementFilter, BLEv42, BT40), 3 by one feature each (HeartRateSensor, BLEv40, NFC), and 3 by six each (the screen and the two members of its atomic set). In the skeleton the atomic set is one node, required directly by three features, hence the row “3, 1”.

How to read the figure. The chart draws such a table for BusyBox, one dot per row: the dot at x=kx = k, y=my = m means “mm features are required by exactly kk others”. Both axes are logarithmic: each step along an axis multiplies by ten (1, 10, 100), so that the many features with few dependants and the few features with many dependants fit in one picture. The features required by nobody (degree 0, 419 of them) cannot be drawn on a logarithmic axis and are left out. Read it from left to right:

  • Top left: 92 features are required by exactly one feature, 44 by two, 14 by three. Most features that are required at all are required by very few.

  • Bottom right: single features (y = 1) with many dependants. The rightmost blue dot is CONFIG_FEATURE_SYSLOG, required by 45 features.

  • The two colours: the blue dots count all the dependants (the complete graph), the orange dots only the direct ones (the skeleton). CONFIG_FEATURE_SYSLOG has 45 dependants but only 15 direct ones: the other 30 reach it through chains. That is why the blue tail reaches further right: a feature high in the hierarchy inherits every dependant below it.

A distribution that falls as a straight line on these axes is the signature of a “power law” (Is it a power law? tests whether it really is one). The dots of BusyBox fall steeply, then scatter at the right, where there is one feature per degree.

The same table for the last month of BusyBox, whose rows are the dots of the chart:

vp_degree_distribution(bb, "requires") |> head(5)
#> # A tibble: 5 x 2
#>   degree features
#>    <int>    <int>
#> 1      0      419
#> 2      1       92
#> 3      2       44
#> 4      3       14
#> 5      4        9
BusyBox, last month: one dot per degree. A dot at (k,m)(k, m) means that mm features are required by exactly kk others; both axes are logarithmic. Blue: all the dependants (complete graph); orange: the direct ones (skeleton). The blue tail is longer: a feature high in the hierarchy inherits every dependant below it.

The Gini coefficient: concentration in one number

What it is. The Gini coefficient comes from economics, where it measures how unequally income is shared in a country: 0 when everyone earns the same, close to 1 when one person earns everything. Here the “income” of a feature is the number of features that require it, and the coefficient measures how unequally the dependencies are shared among the features. Four made-up models of four features, with the required_by of each:

vp_gini(c(3, 3, 3, 3)) # every feature required by three others
#> [1] 0
vp_gini(c(0, 2, 4, 6)) # spread unevenly
#> [1] 0.4167
vp_gini(c(0, 0, 6, 6)) # two features hold everything
#> [1] 0.5
vp_gini(c(0, 0, 0, 12)) # one feature holds everything
#> [1] 0.75

Equal shares give 0; the more the dependants gather on fewer features, the closer the value gets to 1. (With kk features the largest possible value is (k−1)/k(k - 1)/k, here 3/43/4: it reaches 1 only for very many features.) The total does not matter, only how it is shared: the four models have 12 dependants each.

Why it matters.

  • To see whether the model rests on a few foundations. A high Gini means that a handful of features carry most of the dependencies: changing one of them reaches much of the model, so they deserve the most careful review and the most tests, and the model is fragile where they are (see the robustness of Robustness). A low Gini means that the dependencies are spread: no feature is a single point of failure, and no short list of features to watch either.

  • To compare models of different sizes. Two degree distributions of models with 50 and 5,000 features cannot be laid one on the other; their Gini coefficients, which are shares, can.

  • To follow a model through time. A Gini that grows from version to version means that new dependencies keep landing on the same features: the model is centralising around a few hubs. One number per version is easy to plot (vp_history_apply(), Following a model through time); a chart per version is not.

  • For any other quantity. vp_gini() takes any list of numbers: gini_excludes in vp_summary() measures how unevenly the conflicts are spread, and the churn of the features over a history (vp_feature_churn()) can be measured the same way.

On real models:

vp_gini(vp_feature_table(band)$required_by)
#> [1] 0.6494
vp_gini(vp_feature_table(bb)$required_by)
#> [1] 0.8496

The band, 0.65: its dependants gather on the screen and its atomic set. BusyBox, 0.85: much more concentrated; most of its features are required by nobody, and a few, such as CONFIG_FEATURE_SYSLOG, by dozens.

How it is computed: the Lorenz curve. The curve answers one question for every share of the features: the least required features, taken together, hold what share of all the dependants? It is easiest to build it by hand on the band. Sort its features from the least to the most required, and add up as you go:

vp_feature_table(band) |>
  select(feature, required_by) |>
  arrange(required_by) |>
  mutate(
    share_features = row_number() / n(),
    share_dependants = cumsum(required_by) / sum(required_by)
  )
#> # A tibble: 11 x 4
#>    feature            required_by share_features share_dependants
#>    <chr>                    <int>          <dbl>            <dbl>
#>  1 TouchScreen                  0         0.0909           0     
#>  2 ContactlessPayment           0         0.182            0     
#>  3 MovementFilter               0         0.273            0     
#>  4 BLEv42                       0         0.364            0     
#>  5 BT40                         0         0.455            0     
#>  6 HeartRateSensor              1         0.545            0.0476
#>  7 BLEv40                       1         0.636            0.0952
#>  8 NFC                          1         0.727            0.143 
#>  9 Screen                       6         0.818            0.429 
#> 10 OLED                         6         0.909            0.714 
#> 11 CapacityButton               6         1                1

Each row is one point of the curve: xx is share_features, yy is share_dependants. Read three of them:

  • Row 5 (x=0.45x = 0.45, y=0y = 0). The five least required features, almost half of the band, are required by nothing: together they hold none of the 21 dependants. The curve runs flat along the bottom.

  • Row 8 (x=0.73x = 0.73, y=0.14y = 0.14). Add three features required by one feature each: 73 % of the features now hold 3 of the 21 dependants, 14 %.

  • Rows 9 to 11. The last three features, the screen and its atomic set, are required by six features each. They add the remaining 18 dependants, and the curve climbs steeply to (1,1)(1, 1).

The diagonal is what the curve would be if every feature were required by as many features as every other one: then 45 % of the features would hold 45 % of the dependants, and so on. The further the curve sags below the diagonal, the more the dependants are concentrated in a few features. The Gini coefficient measures the sag: it is twice the area between the diagonal and the curve. It is 0 when the curve is the diagonal (everyone equal), and it approaches 1 when one feature holds all the dependants (the curve stays at 0 and jumps up at the last feature). The formula of gini_required_by in the table of vp_summary() above, which vp_gini() computes, is that area counted step by step. In the figure the curve of BusyBox stays near the bottom for longer than that of the band: the 80 % least required features of BusyBox hold only 11 % of all its dependants.

Lorenz curves of required_by. A point (x,y)(x, y) means: the least required xx of the features, taken together, are required by yy of all the dependants (the sum of required_by). The dashed diagonal is perfect equality, every feature required as much as any other; the further a curve sags below it, the more a few features hold all the dependants. The Gini coefficient is twice the area between the diagonal and the curve.

Limits: what this cannot tell you

In the complete requires graph, a feature high in a deep hierarchy is required by everything below it, so long tails, and a high Gini, appear by construction. For the shape of what was written, use the skeleton: vp_degree_distribution(bb, "skeleton"), or the Gini of direct_required_by. The Gini says how concentrated the dependencies are, not which features hold them, nor whether that is good: a deliberate core library and an accidental bottleneck give the same number. Whether a distribution is a “power law” is a statistical question with its own test (Is it a power law?).
